author: Nan Shepherd
en_title: The Living Mountain: The Summit Is Not the End of Looking
zh_deck: 高原、雪下的鼠道、一觉醒来时陌生的景色。谢泼德一次次回到凯恩戈姆，让熟悉的地方继续出现尚未看清的细节。
en_deck: A plateau, tracks emerging from snow, a landscape briefly strange after sleep: Shepherd returns to a familiar place without declaring it fully known.

zh_title: 《活山》：山顶到了，山却还没有看完
zh_body:
把山想成一个尖顶，登山便很容易有了明确的故事：出发，克服困难，终于站到最高处。但谢泼德开篇介绍的凯恩戈姆并不符合这个形状。苏格兰这片山地的高处是一块开阔的高原，山峰并非各自独立的终点。到了上面，还得向下看，才能看见深切的沟壑。

地形改变了行走，也改变了这本书的写法。《活山》并不带我们按日期完成一次旅行。它分别写水、冰雪、空气、动植物、睡眠与人的感受，仿佛一次又一次走入同一片山地，从不同处接近它。读到最后，读者不会得到一条可以完整复走的路线，却会知道，原来一座山有这么多入口。

谢泼德在那里走了许多年。她并非终年隐居深山的人，而是一位教师，也写过小说和诗。工作、家庭与朋友构成她生活的其他部分；山是反复回去的地方。这部薄薄的书写成后搁了三十多年，到1977年才出版。它的时间感也确实不像一份急于发布的旅行见闻：不赶着宣布新发现，更愿意回到曾经看过却仍未看清的东西旁边。

## 雪上留下的，不只有脚印

雪地有时比没有雪的时候更热闹。动物已经离开，足迹却让行走者知道它们来过。谢泼德见到一串忽然出现在空白雪面上的小印记，伸手探查，找到雪下的通道，才明白小鼠从哪里出来。

这个动作使一段看景的文字有了另一种亲近。她没有看见动物本身，仍然通过痕迹接近了它刚才的活动。山地不只在有人观看时发生事情，人来到这里以前，别的生命就已经走过。

而雪又会继续改变这些痕迹。风吹走较松的部分，冻得较实的印记反而留下。原本像凹下去的缺口，后来也可能从雪面上显出来。谢泼德留意的因而不只是“这是谁的脚印”，还有天气怎样接着改写它。

这正是《活山》观察细密的地方。名称可以帮助辨认，却不能替代眼前的形状。我们知道这里有兔、有鼠，并没有因此看完这块雪地；一种生命与一种天气碰在一起，还会留下别的东西。她的文字常常停在这些相遇上，使静止的画面重新有了先后。

读这种自然散文，不需要每段都提炼出人生启示。一串足迹原本就有值得细看的变化。如果太快把它解释成“生命的坚韧”，鼠、雪和风反倒都退到了后面。谢泼德最好的段落，让这些东西先以各自的样子待一会儿。

## 身体一动，景物也跟着变

山不只是摆在远处供人欣赏的形状。谢泼德会改变观看的角度，也写到短睡初醒时，熟悉的地方有一瞬间显得完全陌生。研究者Jared Lindahl讨论这些段落时，特别强调其中身体的参与：并不是把感官放在一边，才进入更深的思考，恰恰是感官的变化打开了新的经验。

“熟悉”通常使生活容易一些。认得路，知道转弯以后是什么，就不用处处留神。但在这里，熟悉也可能使我们太快地认完一个地方。眼前的东西刚出现，旧名称已经替它安排好了位置，目光随即移向别处。

短睡后的片刻不同。位置的知识尚未完全回来，人先遇到颜色、光线和形状，然后才重新想起自己在哪里。谢泼德把这样短促的时刻写下来，并不是声称忘记知识就比较高明。它让人发觉，平常的认识已经替观看做了多少整理，而这种整理并非眼前事物的全部。

所以，《活山》不大适合用几个观点代替。说“多用感官认识世界”，意思似乎已经有了；可这个人怎样走、怎样停，醒来时怎样重新遇见熟悉的环境，还得靠文字慢慢呈现。观察不是观点后面的配图，它本身就在推动认识。

这也解释了书中一种难以说清的亲密：有时她仿佛不再站在外面看山，而是身在其中。她并没有因此主张山具有人的意识。在“睡眠”的段落里，她还特意抵住这种拟人化的想象。感到自己进入了山的生活，不必再添加一个有意向人传授智慧的山神。

读者可以停在经验本身，不急着替它找到宗教或哲学上的归属。它毕竟不是一套按步骤重复就会得到相同结果的练习。重要的是这个作者怎样努力说清自己遭遇了什么，以及她在说不清的时候，仍愿意保留那一点不确定。

## 她并不反对费力

谢泼德常被放在“征服高峰”的反面介绍。这样的区别有根据，但若把她读成反对目标、只赞美漫游，就又过于简单。她虽然不喜欢把登山完全变成比赛，却承认追求纪录的人也可能深爱山地，并且具有可敬的本领。

这一点使书的尺度宽了起来。她批评的是山被缩减为战绩，并非力气花得太多。一个人愿意认真练习，寻找难走的路线，完全可能在过程中更懂自己的身体，也更懂岩石。走得轻松与认识得深入，并不总是一回事。

从这儿看，《活山》与一些“逃离忙碌”的想象颇不相同。山里也有辛苦，行走也需要专注和耐心。没有人替她消除劳累，她也不总把劳累视为应该尽快省掉的成本。自己愿意进入一件事，与不得不完成一项任务，可能都使身体疲倦，感受却不同。

不过，亲近并没有让山失去危险。书中写到战争时期坠毁的飞机，残骸使风景中留着战争的痕迹。与前面那些喜悦放在一起读，山便不只是供人寻求宁静的地方。

这段材料尤其重要，因为它打断了一种容易形成的阅读幻觉：仿佛只要不抱着征服的态度，山就会温柔地接纳我们。地形、云雾和天气不会因为人的心意而改变。感受很强烈，不等于判断已经正确；再深的喜爱，也不能代替辨认条件的本领。

《活山》并不是户外安全指南，读者不应拿它安排路线。它给予的，是一种更复杂的关系：地方使人喜悦，也要求人承认自己并不能掌握它。二者在同一本书里，并未互相取消。

## 水为什么还要回去看

谢泼德写溪水的澄澈，觉得有些亮度离开后很难仅凭记忆重新唤起，得再回去看。这里没有发现一条新河，也没有完成前人没走过的路。她面对的，是认识之后仍会失去的东西。

我们通常把知识理解成积累：去过一个地方，便多知道一点；再去一次，应当再增加一点。《活山》却容许另一种往返。有些经验不能被完整带走，不是因为上次不够专心，而是因为光线、身体和眼前的水本来就不可能原封不动地存进记忆。

这样说，也没有贬低记忆。恰恰因为还记得那种明亮，人会再去；而再去又发现，记得的并不能完全代替所见。书中的重复于是具有一种特别的推进方式：不是抵达更多地方，而是不断修正自己以为已经知道的地方。

这使它的缓慢有了理由。若期待连续事件、险情和结局，读者可能觉得章节总在绕回来；若愿意随着不同的感官停留，便会渐渐辨认出这些“回来”的差异。水、雪、睡眠不是几个可以随意交换的题目，它们分别让山以不同的方式出现。

珍妮特·温特森谈过自己的阅读经验：她原本不是登山爱好者，也不熟悉凯恩戈姆，仍能通过这本书进入那个世界。这个回应颇能说明自然写作的力量。读者不必已经过着作者的生活，文字仍能让人接近一种陌生的注意方式。

但谢泼德的价值也不只在于替没去过的人提供风景。她让一个认识地方很久的人继续显得好奇，甚至继续显得不够知道。经验丰富，并没有使她可以轻易说“山就是这样”。她知道的越多，越有具体的东西需要再看。

书到这里，山顶已不再是最重要的句号。我们记住的可能是一串从雪下出现的足迹，也可能是一觉醒来，眼前景色尚未恢复旧名称的片刻。它们很小，却使这座山不再只是远方的轮廓。谢泼德把多年行走留在书中，并没有宣告认识已经完成；读者因此也愿意随她再走一段。
en_body:
Imagine a mountain as a pointed summit and climbing supplies an obvious story: set out, overcome difficulties, reach the highest place. But the Cairngorms Nan Shepherd introduces at the beginning of The Living Mountain do not fit that shape. Their high ground forms an open plateau rather than a collection of isolated destinations. Once up there, one must look down to see the deeply cut hollows.

The terrain changes both walking and writing. The book does not lead us through one journey in date order. It approaches water, snow and ice, air, animals and plants, sleep, and bodily experience, repeatedly entering the same landscape by different means. At the end we have no single route to retrace, but a sense of how many ways there are into a mountain.

Shepherd walked there for many years. She was not a year-round mountain recluse: she taught and wrote novels and poetry, with work, family, and friends constituting other parts of life. The hills were somewhere to return. Written in the 1940s, this short book waited more than thirty years for publication in 1977. Its sense of time indeed differs from a travel dispatch eager to announce discoveries. It prefers returning to things already seen but not yet fully understood.

## Snow holds more than footprints

A snowfield may contain more visible activity than bare ground. Animals are gone, but their tracks tell a walker they were there. Shepherd finds tiny marks appearing abruptly on an otherwise blank surface. Investigating, she discovers the passage beneath the snow from which a mouse has emerged.

The movement changes a scenic description into another kind of encounter. Without seeing the animal, she approaches its recent activity through traces. The landscape does not begin happening when a human arrives to observe it. Other lives have been moving through it already.

Snow continues to alter those traces. Wind removes looser material while more firmly frozen impressions remain. What began as a depression may later stand out above the surface. Shepherd notices not only which creature made the track but what weather subsequently does to it.

This is the precision of her observation. Names aid recognition without replacing the shape before us. Knowing there are mice and hares does not finish our looking. A kind of life and a kind of weather meet and leave something further. Her prose attends to the encounter, restoring sequence to what first appeared a still scene.

There is no need to extract a lesson about life from every passage. The changing tracks are worth seeing in themselves. Call them evidence of resilience too quickly and mouse, snow, and wind recede. The strongest nature writing here allows things to remain particular for a while.

## When the body shifts, the scene shifts too

The mountain is not simply a distant shape presented for appreciation. Shepherd alters her angle of vision and describes waking from a brief sleep to find a familiar place momentarily strange. Discussing these passages, scholar Jared Lindahl emphasizes the body’s participation. Deeper reflection does not arrive by discarding the senses; changes in sensation open another experience.

Familiarity generally makes life easier. Knowing the path and what comes after a turn means we need not attend to everything. Here, though, it can also make recognition too quick. Before something has fully appeared, an old name has assigned it a place and the eye has moved on.

The instant after sleep is different. Knowledge of location has not quite returned. Color, light, and shape precede remembering where one is. Recording this does not make Shepherd an advocate of forgetting knowledge. It reveals how much organizing ordinary recognition has already done, and how that organization fails to exhaust what is present.

This is why a few propositions cannot substitute for the book. “Know the world through the senses” seems to state the point. But how this person walks and stops, how waking brings her into a familiar place again, must unfold in language. Observation is not a picture appended to an argument. It is part of how understanding develops.

At times she seems less outside the mountain looking at it than within its life. This does not require claiming that the mountain has human consciousness. In the discussion of sleep she resists that anthropomorphic conclusion. An intimate experience of place need not add a mountain spirit intending to teach us wisdom.

Readers can remain with the experience without immediately deciding its philosophical or religious affiliation. It is not a reproducible exercise whose steps guarantee identical results. What matters is a writer’s effort to describe what happened and to retain some uncertainty where description falls short.

## Effort is not the enemy

Shepherd is often introduced as an alternative to conquering peaks. The contrast has grounds, but becomes too simple if it makes her an opponent of purpose who praises only wandering. Though she resists reducing climbing to competition, she acknowledges that record-seekers may love mountains deeply and possess admirable skills.

This enlarges the book’s judgment. What she challenges is the reduction of a place to a record, not excessive expenditure of effort. Serious practice and difficult routes may bring someone to understand both a body and a rock face better. Ease and depth of acquaintance do not necessarily coincide.

Seen this way, the book differs from fantasies of escaping busyness. The hills contain hard work too; walking asks for concentration and patience. No one removes the labor for her, and she does not always treat fatigue as a cost to minimize. Freely entering something and being obliged to complete a task can both tire the body without feeling the same.

Intimacy does not remove danger. The book includes aircraft wreckage from wartime, leaving traces of war in the landscape. Read beside its pleasures, this prevents the mountain from becoming merely a place supplied for human tranquility.

Such material interrupts an attractive illusion: that relinquishing conquest will ensure a gentle welcome. Terrain, fog, and weather do not change in response to good intentions. Intensity of feeling does not prove sound judgment. Deep affection still needs the ability to recognize conditions.

The Living Mountain is not a guide for planning a safe route. It offers a more complex relationship: a place can bring joy while requiring acknowledgment that we cannot master it. Neither experience cancels the other.

## Why return to look at water?

Shepherd writes of clear streams whose brightness is difficult to summon from memory after leaving. She needs to see them again. There is no discovery of a new river here, no unprecedented route. What interests her is something that can be lost even after acquaintance.

We generally think of knowledge as accumulation. Visiting a place adds to what we know; visiting again should add more. The book allows another kind of return. Some experiences cannot be carried away intact, not because we were insufficiently attentive, but because light, body, and water cannot be stored unchanged in memory.

That does not disparage memory. Remembering the brightness encourages a return; returning reveals that memory cannot entirely replace seeing. Repetition gives the book its distinctive movement. It advances less by reaching more places than by revising what seemed already known about one.

Its slowness consequently has a purpose. Readers expecting continuous events, emergencies, and resolution may feel the chapters circle back. Those willing to pause with different senses begin to recognize differences within the returns. Water, snow, and sleep are not interchangeable themes. Each makes the mountain appear differently.

Jeanette Winterson has described being drawn into the book despite not being a mountaineer or knowing the Cairngorms. Her response suggests what nature writing can do. A reader need not already inhabit the writer’s life to approach an unfamiliar way of attending through words.

Nor is Shepherd valuable only as a supplier of scenery for people unable to go. She allows someone long acquainted with a place to remain curious, even insufficiently knowledgeable. Experience never licenses her simply to declare that this is what mountains are. The more she knows, the more particular things require another look.

By now the summit is no longer the most important full stop. We may remember tracks emerging from beneath snow, or the instant after waking before a landscape resumes its old names. These are small experiences, but they keep the mountain from remaining a distant outline. Shepherd leaves years of walking in her book without announcing that understanding is finished. The reader is therefore willing to walk a little farther with her.
